To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) art-naïve observers are sensitive to color and spatial structures in art, (b) their color and spatial preferences are not random but systematic, and (c) their color and orientation preferences are influenced by cultural background.

“art-naive” observers are sensitive and responsive to the color composition and spatial balance of abstract art and that the perceived balance point of a painting influences the preference for the original versus reversed orientation.
the perception of abstract art in art-naive participants is influenced by their cultural background.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether abstract paintings are perceived in a universal or a cultural-specific way.
the question of how much the “eye of the beholder” is free to interpret abstract art.
the question of whether the “eye of the beholder” is truly free or rather constrained by the artwork and/or by the observer’s cultural background.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the “eye of the beholder” is not free in the perception of abstract art, but is guided by cultural and artistic experience.
the eye of the beholder is not as free as one might think.
“Kandinsky or me?” is not a question of either-or but a question of how and why.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the “eye of the beholder” in abstract art is more free than we thought, but less than we might have expected.
“the eye is not as free as we think it is” (Wagemans et al., 2012, p. 3).
the eye of the beholder is less free than it may seem at first glance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
abstract art is not as free from cultural influences as previously thought.
, even though art is an expression of the artist, it can also be an expression of the viewer.
the perception of abstract art is not as free and open-ended as it may seem at first glance.
